To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the radiation of the ecologically dominant group Symbiodinium in reef‐building scleractinian corals was driven by host specialization, and that this radiation was triggered by major climate changes in the Miocene and Pliocene epochs.

1) Symbiodinium species are ecologically and evolutionarily diverse; 2) host specialization is a key driver of Symbiodinium radiation; 3) the radiation of Symbiodiniun Clade C is largely post‐Miocene, and; 4) Symbiodiniuim Clade C species diversity is a product of “boom and busts” during major climate shifts.
the radiation of reef coral endosymbiotic microbes was driven primarily by host specialization and was associated with major climate changes in the Atlantic Ocean.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the evolutionary ecology of a microbial symbiont that is ecologically dominant in the marine environment and has profound implications for the health of coral reefs worldwide.
the evolution of the most abundant and ecologically dominant symbiotic dinoflagelate in reef corals.
the evolutionary ecology of a microbial symbiont that has been instrumental in shaping the ecology, biogeography, and evolution of a major animal clade.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

there is a high degree of host specificity in the Symbiodinium species, and that the diversification of the Symbiodinum is driven by the diversification of its host corals, and that the host coral diversification is in turn driven by climate change.
the adaptive radiation of reef coral symbionts was driven primarily by host specialization.
the radiation of reef‐building coralline algae is the result of the radiation of their endosymbiotic algae, Symbiodinum.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
Symbiodinum diversification has been driven by host‐specialization and climate‐change.
the most dominant endosymbionts of reef corals, which are critical to the health of coral reef ecosystems, are a diverse assemblage of species that have undergone recent adaptive radiation.
Symbiodinum Clade C is a diverse and ecologically dominant radiation of reef‐building coralline dinoflagellate endosymbionts.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the adaptive radiation of reef‐building endosymbionts has been shaped by both regional and global environmental factors.
the evolutionary dynamics of eukaryote microbes may be driven by the same ecological and historical forces that shape macroscopic biodiversity.
Symbiodium Clade C represents a classic adaptive radiation of microbial eukaryotes, which is a major finding in microbial ecology.
